en: A Brief Commentary on the *Buddhabhāṣita-urundabhadra-pūtra-sūtra* △ Text Part Two: First, the Title.
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Urundabhadra Bowl*.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, Dharma Master Dharmakṣema translated the *Ullambana Sūtra*. "Ullambana" is a term from the Western Regions; here it means "hanging upside down.
"Pén" (basin), according to the Tripiṭaka masters of the Tang, is translated as "vessel for salvation. Following local custom, it should be called the "Vessel for Saving Those Hanging Upside Down.
Part Two: The Main Text, in three sections. First, the Introductory Section, in two parts. First, the *Śraddhā-pratyaya-nidāna* (Preface of Authentication).
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Although six conditions were lacking for the assembly, he remained silent; yet, had he spoken, he would certainly have been accompanied by his retinue. Therefore, the end of the sutra says:

The fourfold assembly of disciples rejoiced and practiced accordingly. Regarding the opening phrase "Thus have I heard," which distinguishes this scripture from others: these variations are each the intent of the respective translators.
Some say, "Such a Dharma as this I have heard from the Buddha," while others say, "I have heard such a Dharma from the side of the Buddha.
Both are terms used to point to the Dharma. The reason for not using the first-person pronoun "I" is intended to manifest the sanctity [of the teaching].

This is because all people have realized the principle of non-self (*anātman*). As for the mention of this in other sūtras, it refers to Ānanda pointing to the conventional person (*pudgala*) composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*);
it is not the same as the self imagined by ordinary people, and thus there is no fault. Regarding the Jetavana and so forth:
the Elder [Anāthapiṇḍada] purchased the grove with gold, but there was a small corner remaining. The Prince then offered the remainder of his land, and a gatehouse was erected. He made the offering.
The trees in the garden formed a forested shade. △ Second, the introductory section on the occasion of the event has six parts. First, Maudgalyāyana’s attainment of the Way:
Mahāmaudgalyāyana had just attained the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
The clan name of Maudgalyāyana is Mudgalun in the language of Tang, which means "green-gram" (mudga). In ancient times, there was a rishi in that country who constantly ate green gram;
therefore, he took it as his clan name. The Venerable One belonged to that lineage. His personal name was Nyagrodha, which is the name of a tree;
because he was born through the sacrifice of this tree deity, he was named after it. However, the people of that time held him in high esteem...

Therefore, he was made to call himself by his clan name. As for "one who has first attained the six supernatural powers": having first attained the Noble Path, he immediately delivered his two parents.
It is because one originally cultivates the Way on account of one's parents that this occurs. Although the Way is without distinction, individual original vows differ;
it is not necessarily the case that all sages act in this manner. △ Second, knowing gratitude and desiring to repay it.
"Desiring to deliver one's parents to repay the kindness of nursing.

In the first phrase, "parents" are mentioned collectively; in the second phrase, emphasis is placed specifically on the mother. Delivering them to liberation is precisely what constitutes repaying their kindness.
△ Third, longing and searching:
one immediately observes the world with the eye of the Path (*mārga-cakṣus*).

This observation of the world is the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣur-abhijñā*); because it is attained through the realization of the Path, it is called the "eye of the Path. △ Fourth.
One is able to see their location.
Seeing their parents born among the hungry ghosts (preta), they do not see food or drink; their skin and bones stand joined together.
Being born among the hungry ghosts is the ripened fruit (vipākaphala) that compensates for the projecting karma (ākṣepaka-karma). Not seeing food and drink is the concordant fruit (niṣyandaphala).
The fruit [of ripening] is so called because it recompenses the completing karma (*pūrṇakarma*). That the skin and bones stand joined together is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, the primary abode of the hungry ghosts (*preta*) is located five hundred *yojanas* beneath this continent, with the same dimensions in length and breadth; there exists the realm of Yamarāja.
For humans, one month constitutes a single day; by this reckoning, months and years accumulate until their lifespan reaches five hundred years.
△ Fifth, Wailing and Going to Rescue:
Maudgalyāyana was filled with grief and sorrow, and he immediately took his alms-bowl, filled it with rice, and went to provide food for his mother.
The *Sanzang ke* states: "Cruel anguish. The commentary explains: "The emotion stirs to the very marrow of one's bones; the wailing cries shake heaven and earth.
△ Sixth, the manifestation of evil habits.

When her mother obtained the bowl of rice, she shielded the bowl with her left hand while grasping the food with her right hand to eat it. Before the food had even entered her mouth, it transformed into glowing embers, so that she could not eat.

She shielded the bowl with her left hand out of stinginess, fearing others would encroach upon it; she grasped the food with her right hand out of greed for her own sustenance, clutching and seizing it.
Furthermore, as stinginess and greed are so vehement that they manifest in this way, how can one overcome these circumstances when provided with inferior food and drink?
The preceding section on the introduction is concluded. △ Second, the main body of the teaching has two parts. First, Maudgalyāyana compassionately describes their suffering and distress.
Maudgalyāyana cried out in lamentation, weeping and wailing as he hurried back to report this in detail to the Buddha.
A son must urgently inform his father; a minister must urgently inform his sovereign. When one’s own strength is insufficient, it is only right to seek refuge in the Buddha.
II. The Tathāgata Extensively Reveals the Causes and Conditions (in eight parts): 1. Manifesting the Profundity of the Mother’s Transgression.
The Buddha said, "The roots of your mother's transgressions are deep and firmly entangled.
According to a sutra, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Maudgalyāyana was named Rābu and his mother’s name was Qingti.
After Rābu had gone out, he instructed his mother, saying, 'If any guests should arrive, you must prepare a meal for them. After he had departed, guests arrived, and so the mother—"
She did not provide them. Instead, she again falsely prepared a feast for food. When her son returned and asked, "Guests came yesterday; how did you prepare for them?
his mother said, "Did you not see the place where the food was set out? From that time until now, through five hundred lifetimes, stinginess has continued in succession;
therefore it is said that the roots of his transgressions are deeply entangled. Question: Since the era of Dīpaṃkara Buddha...
Question: "The mothers from whom one has been born are not one and the same; why then do you single out to save that Ceti? Answer:
"Ceti’s karmic affinity with Maudgalyāyana is profound; in this present life, she is once again his mother. One merely saves the mother who gave birth to this current body;
it does not mean saving that Ceti of a distant past. Other such arguments are all based on a failure to reach the truth. II. Clarifying the Child.
Your virtue is inferior;
it is not something that can be remedied by your power alone.
Your mother’s stinginess was directed toward everything, spanning many lifetimes and involving many people; how could you possibly [remedy this] alone?
Human effort can provide rescue and salvation. △ Third, the refutation of the powerlessness of heterodoxy:

"Though your filial piety may move heaven and earth, neither the celestial deities, the terrestrial spirits, the heterodox demons and external paths, the Daoist masters, nor the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings can do anything about it."
The Tripitaka Master said: "Even if you were to move celestial spirits in the upper realms and rouse earth deities in the lower regions;

even if you were to capture malevolent demons and ensnare heretics from all sides; even if you were to unify the six directions under one house and consolidate the eight classes of beings into a single assembly—were you to combine all such supernatural powers, you still could do nothing about it, O Daoist. You are merely a Daoist among those who follow the way of external paths. (4)
This demonstrates that there is indeed efficacy [in the Dharma].
One must rely upon the majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Saṃgha of the ten directions to attain liberation.
As the Tripiṭaka states: "A single thread cannot restrain an elephant; one must depend on many strands. A single person cannot restrain karma."
One must certainly rely upon manifold virtues. △ Fifth, the promise of the means of rescue:
"I shall now proclaim the Dharma of rescue so that all who encounter difficulties may be freed from sorrow and suffering;
not only shall your mother be freed from suffering, but she shall also be freed from all sorrows and sufferings. △ Sixth, the demonstration of the True Dharma.

II. First, the method for instructing disciples in making offerings has five parts. First, determining the superior time: the day of the *pravāraṇā* (the end of the rainy season retreat) is the superior time.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when the monks of the ten directions perform the *pravāraṇā*, this is the superior time."
“Seng zizì” (The Sangha’s *prātimokṣa*). The word “seng” (sangha) is used as a term of respect for the assembly of monks; this is an error on the part of the translator.
Why not say, instead, “at the time of the communal *prātimokṣa*”? As for *prātimokṣa*: it means to allow one’s own faults to be freely pointed out by others.

This refers to the fact that although one has carefully guarded the "raft" throughout the summer retreat, there is still fear of being deluded while acting as the central figure; one must certainly rely upon those observing from the sidelines.
Regarding gain and loss, he bared his shoulder amidst the assembly and said:
"Virtuous Elders, if you have seen my transgression, heard of my offense, or suspect me of having committed one, please feel free to point it out. Out of compassion, speak to me; I shall confess."
In this way, both body and mind are purified. One who makes offerings to these [images] rescues the deceased from the past and provides sustenance for those currently living.

Thus, the Tripitaka Master said: "On the day monks observe the *varṣā* (the end of the rainy season retreat) and when the great assembly performs the *pravāraṇā* (the invitation to point out faults), many members of the Sangha attain the Way;
such individuals among the four fruits of arhatship can rescue those in distress for seven generations. 2. Generating a Superior Intention: Filial Piety as the Motive.
"Śreyas, you should [act] for the sake of your parents of seven lifetimes past and those currently in distress.

As for 'seven lifetimes,' this is what is followed in the Confucian tradition, which takes the physical form as fundamental and transmits the substance through continuous succession from father to son."
The above is for the sake of honoring seven generations; thus, the father is especially revered. This is the primary tenet of the Buddha’s teaching:

that the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the fundamental essence, while the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their physical forms serve as the support for this spiritual consciousness. In every successive life, one has parents who give birth to and nourish this body.
From the present life back through seven previous births, the parents from whom one was born constitute these "seven generations. Thus, [the spirit] relies upon them...
The place where one dwells is solely within the mother’s womb; from birth, it is also mostly the mother who provides nourishment through breastfeeding and embraces one in her arms.
Therefore, one is especially indebted to the mother. For this reason, the sūtras speak only of repaying the debt of nursing. The Tripiṭaka Master said: "Heaven covers and earth sustains."

Having no fear of toil and hardship, those submerged in the realms of the hidden and the manifest ought, by principle, to repay their boundless debt of gratitude. △ Third, the offering of supreme provisions:
the hundred flavors and five fruits constitute the supreme offering.
Providing food of a hundred flavors, the five fruits, water jars for rinsing, fragrant oil, lamps and candles, couches, mats, and bedding—
placing all the sweet delicacies of the world within these vessels— to make offerings to the assembly of virtuous monks of the ten directions.
Rice serves as the principal element among the hundred flavors; "hundred" is a large number and does not refer to a fixed count of one hundred.
There are five types of fruits: first, stone fruits; second, skin fruits; third, shell fruits; fourth, husked grains such as sesame and hempseed; and fifth, pods such as water chestnuts and beans.
The basins for drawing and pouring water are those used for bathing; when placed within the basin, it is precisely what is meant by the *ulambana-piṇḍa*.
Furthermore, as for how the beds and other items may be placed within the basin, they should be offered within the context of the *Ullambana* (Alaṃbana) offering assembly.
The Tripiṭaka Master said: "You must employ the four requisites of material offerings and the eight delicacies of the basin;
extend your visualization throughout the ten directions and perform the offering with a clarified single mind. 4. Praising the Supreme Field: The noble sages constitute the supreme field.

On this day, all the assembly of holy ones— some in mountain retreats absorbed in meditative concentration, some having attained the fruits of the four paths, some walking in meditation beneath trees,
some freely exercising the six supernormal powers to teach and transform śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,

and some great beings who are bodhisattvas of the ten stages manifesting as bhikṣus by means of skillful expedients— all within the great assembly were of one mind, receiving the *pātra-bhara* (alms) food.
The path of the noble assembly, endowed with pure precepts, possesses a vast and boundless virtue.
*Pātra-bhājana* refers to the food in the bowl; in Sanskrit it is called *pātra*, which here means "measured vessel. The character *he* (和) is an error.
Nowadays, it is simply called *bō* (鉢), which is an abbreviation. The title of the sutra uses the character *pén* (盆), which is the same as *bō*. Translation.

At that time, following worldly custom, it was called a "basin" (*pen*). Both the basin and the bowl (*patra*) are vessels; therefore, the Tripitaka Master explained the title by translating it as "vessel for salvation.
△ Fifth, the attainment of supreme benefit: the deceased parents are freed from suffering and reborn in heaven, which constitutes the supreme benefit.

Those who make offerings to such monks during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony will, in this present life, see their parents, six types of relatives, and kinsmen escape the sufferings of the three miserable realms and attain liberation at that very moment.
Their clothing and food will appear spontaneously. If their parents are still living, they shall enjoy happiness and prosperity for a hundred years;

if their ancestors up to the seventh generation have been reborn in heaven, they will dwell there with sovereign ease, being born through transformation amidst the radiant flowers of the celestial realm.
"These monks who are invited to the *pravāraṇā*" refers to the aforementioned "field of excellence. The phrase "in this present life... [refers to] being freed from suffering;

the phrase "if one serves one's parents... [refers to] attaining happiness. As for the single phrase "food and clothing come naturally," since it reverses birth in the three miserable realms and leads to rebirth in the human or heavenly realms, it belongs to the section on "extracting from suffering.
Alternatively, "attaining happiness" may also belong to the subsequent section. First, regarding the present life and one's parents:
It is said that they are "of the present life" because they are the parents who gave birth to this body; it does not mean that those who have not yet passed away are called "of the present life.

Therefore, the attainment of benefit is specifically indicated as "exiting the three miserable realms," whereas the text itself contains its own passage below regarding parents who are currently living and have not yet passed away.
Therefore, it is said that the benefit received is "happiness and merit for a hundred years. △ Second, the ritual for instructing the assembly of monks in receiving offerings:

At that time, the Buddha commanded the monks from the ten directions to first offer a prayer of blessing (*paritta*) on behalf of the donor’s family, wishing that their parents of seven generations may practice the mind of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and only then receive the food. When first receiving the food, they must first place it before the Buddha in the stupa or monastery.
After the assembly of monks has finished the ritual of incantation and prayer before the Buddha, they partake of the food themselves.

The first half [of the ritual] purifies the three karmas: the karma of speech through incantation and prayer; the karma of mind through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and the karma of body through partaking of the food.
The second half embodies the Three Jewels: the stupa represents the Buddha; the incantation and prayer represent the Dharma; and partaking of the food represents the Saṃgha. As for the stupa:
The term "intention" (*yi*) applies to both the halls and the stupas; the stupas enshrine the *śarīra*, while the halls enshrine the Buddha images. △ Seventh, the filial son attains realization:
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and the assembly of great bodhisattvas were all filled with great joy; Maudgalyāyana’s weeping and sobbing ceased entirely.
Since her pure karma had been accomplished, she knew she would surely be freed from suffering; thus, she rejoiced and ceased weeping. △ Eighth, the Mother’s Attainment of Benefit:
At that time, on that very day, Maudgalyāyana’s mother was immediately liberated from all the sufferings of the hungry ghosts.
First, one receives the teaching and attains realization; next, one prepares the *bōng* (vessel) offerings; finally, one shall obtain benefit and attain realization.
The subsequent phrase "then one is liberated from suffering" is an omission in the translation of the sutra. It should follow the text of the compilers as follows:
"At that time, after Maudgalyāyana had heard this Dharma, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he prepared the *bōng* offerings and made them to the Saṃgha during the *pravāraṇā*."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana’s mother was liberated from all the sufferings of the hungry ghosts on that very day; thus, both the words and their meaning are clearly revealed.
The Tripiṭaka Master says: "Once the filial son has presented offerings on this morning, the compassionate mother is thereby rid of her calamities.
This concludes the Section on the Correct Teaching.
△ Third, the section on circulation (pariṇāmanā) has three parts. First, the formal request:

Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Because my mother, who gave me birth, has been able to receive the power of the merit of the Triple Gem and the majestic spiritual power of the Saṃgha, all disciples of the Buddhas in future ages should likewise offer the *bowl-liberation* (*ulambana*)."
"Can this rite of *pūrna* (the alms-bowl) for the salvation of present parents, and even those up to seven generations of ancestors, be performed?
When these words were spoken, it was also after the offerings had been presented; it was not the business of a single session.
It was only upon reaching the Pipphalavana Cave that they finally assembled [the teachings] into a sutra. △ Second, the Praise and Request.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, most excellent! You have asked me well; I was just about to speak, yet you ask again.
'Excellent, most excellent' means that [your question] deeply accords with the Sage's mind. The following two phrases explain the reason for this. △ Third, the response to the request has five parts.
First, the instruction on initiating practice.
"Good son, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, kings, crown princes, ministers, high officials, the three dukes, the myriad officials,
or commoners who practice kindness and filial piety, they should all first, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month—
the day of the Buddha’s joy and the day of the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā*— for the sake of their present parents and their parents of the past seven generations,"
One offers food of a hundred flavors within the *uḷambana* bowl as a gift to the monks of the ten directions who have completed their retreat.

On this day of joy, when the ninety-day period of intensive practice for the bhikṣus has reached its conclusion, they become even more earnest and sincere, fulfilling the original intention of the Buddha.
How could one not rejoice? △ Second, the instruction to make a vow:
"I vow that my present parents shall live for a hundred years, free from illness and all suffering and affliction;
furthermore, that my parents of up to seven generations shall be freed from the suffering of the hungry ghosts and be reborn among humans and devas, where their merit and joy are boundless."
A "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to the heart’s aspiration and desire. It is the wish that both the living and the deceased may all find happiness. △ Third, the instruction on constant practice:
Those who are disciples of the Buddha and cultivate filial piety should, in every thought-moment, constantly remember their parents, even up to their ancestors of seven generations.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month each year, they should always use filiality and compassion to remember their biological parents and perform [this rite] for them.

To offer the *Ullambana* alms to the Buddha and the Sangha in order to repay the kindness of one's parents who nurtured one with love and compassion is for those disciples of the Buddha who practice filial piety;
conversely, this clarifies that it is not for those who are not disciples of the Buddha or those who are unfilial.
Furthermore, this may also refer to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and even the common people mentioned above in the section on "Arising in Practice."
People who practice benevolence and filial piety—why is this? Because they have heard what the Buddha has taught and act according to those teachings, they are all disciples of the Buddha.
Therefore, in the petitions above and the observances below, it is stated everywhere that these are "all disciples of the Buddha."

The Tripitaka Master said: "Since the bonds of parental affection do not leave the mind for even a single thought-moment, a filial child seeking to repay this kindness must provide offerings year after year without ceasing.
△ Fourth, exhortation to accept and uphold [the teaching].
If all disciples of the Buddha should uphold this Dharma:

the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that one receives it by the power of faith and maintains it by the power of mindfulness; "to receive" (*feng*) is synonymous with "to accept. △ Fifth, receiving the command with joy.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana and his fourfold assembly of disciples joyfully received and practiced [the teaching].
The "fourfold assembly" refers to the monastics—monks and nuns—and the laity—men and women; alternatively, it may refer to humans, devas, nāgas, and ghosts.
Recorded by the śrāmaṇera Yuánqí of Mount Cáoxī.
Regarding this commentary: Master Guifeng had been making offerings to the Triple Gem on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony for many years and, concurrently, lectured upon its text.
Consequently, he returned to his hometown and established it according to the [standard] liturgy. Elders among both the clergy and the laity, moved by both grief and joy, followed its practice;

with one voice and in unison, they requested the composition of a new commentary. This was done to grant their request and to elucidate the essential path. However, as for those various additions and suspensions...

To speak of it as being like the *Avataṃsaka* or the *Complete Enlightenment* (Pūrṇabodhi) sūtras, where great compassion flows forth—this is indeed so. However, this sūtra concerns the causes and effects for humans and devas;
one need only rely upon its teachings and put them into practice. There is no necessity for extensive exposition. Now, let us proceed to the commentary on the text.
There are many citations [in this work], which cause beginners of shallow learning to withdraw even before they have had the opportunity to survey its contents.

Therefore, I have made a brief excerpt of the direct exegesis, intending to ensure that the text and meaning are concise, accessible, and clear. This is not intended as a presentation of my own personal views;
may readers refrain from being overly critical. Written on the fifth day of the fifth month in the Gengchen year of the Da Qing Guangxu era by Kobayashi.
Written by his disciple Hyong in the Hall of Radiant Light within the Stupa Pavilion of the Fotu Hermitage in Yangzhou.
